newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU likely to extend beer, oil sales rules.
newsitem.headline: EU likely to extend beer, oil sales rules.

text.p: The European Commission is expected to extend rules exempting exclusive supply and distribution agreements in the beer and oil industries from fair competition rules, Commission and industry sources said.
The largely expected decision is made necessary by the Commission's successive delays in adopting a consultation paper on how to deal with such sales arrangements on a long-lasting basis.
The so-called European Union beer block exemption, which also covers petrol service stations, is due to expire at the end of 1997.
An industry source speaking on the condition of anonymity told Reuters it could be extended by two years.

A Commission competition official said this did "not seem unreasonable". But another source close to European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert warned the decision to give the industry a grace period had not been taken. Nor had it been decided how long that period would be.
British brewers have been particularly concerned at the prospect of loosing the beer block exemption.
The rules adopted in 1983 exempt beer-supply arrangements between British breweries and pubs owned by them -- usually described as tied houses -- from competition rules.
The British beer market is unique in the European Union in that the vast majority of pubs are owned by powerful brewers which insist they only sell their products.
The British government in the late 80s relaxed brewers' grip on pub tenants by adopting legislation allowing for a guest beer.
But even this was questioned recently by the Commission on the grounds that it put European continental beers at a disadvantage.
The expected extension of the beer-supply exemption is set to be greeted by British brewers who are in disarray over the legal uncertainty created by both moves.

The Commission is expected to adopt its controversial green paper on exclusive supply and distribution agreements -- also known as the vertical restraints paper -- before the end of the year. This is more than a year later than initially due.
The paper, which will be submitted to a wide consulting process, is also due to address the issue of franchising covered by a separate block exemption which expires at the end of 1999.

Van Miert said recently in reply to a question by British Socialist member of the European Parliament David Thomas that the green paper will contain several options for the future. This includes carrying on with sectoral block exemptions or adopting general rules based on the market share of the companies entering into restrictive agreements.

Van Miert said he would allow for "several months" of consultation of all interested parties. British brewers have already made it known they would like a renewal of the block exemption for a minimum of 15 years.
